title: Driving on Memory
claim: A camera-free baseline that retrieves stored memories nearly matches full perception-based models, so the benchmark barely requires reacting to the current scene.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; three pipelines plus a bar chart of scores
description: A 2x2 grid of gray panels. Top-left shows a standard end-to-end model like DrivoR. Multi-camera images and an ego-status box (velocity, acceleration, command) feed Perception and a Planner, which outputs a car with predicted trajectories. Bottom-left shows the Ego Status MLP baseline. A crossed-out orange camera marks 'No perception', and ego status goes straight to the Planner. Bottom-right shows MemoryDrivoR (ours). It also has a crossed-out camera, but absolute pose queries a 'Memories of training drives' database and this feeds the Planner together with ego status. Top-right is a grouped bar chart of PDMS and EPDMS on NAVSIMv1 and NAVSIMv2. DrivoR is blue, Ego Status MLP orange and MemoryDrivoR green. Ego Status MLP scores far lower, while MemoryDrivoR is close to DrivoR. Blue boxes mark inputs and orange marks the removed perception.
caption: MemoryDrivoR. We introduce a novel analytic baseline for testing how much benchmark performance depends on camera input from the evaluated scene. MemoryDrivoR replaces camera input with memories from previous sensor-rich traversals. These memories carry static information but cannot describe the dynamics of the current traffic scene. In contrast to other baselines without cameras such as Ego Status MLP [ref], MemoryDrivoR achieves surprisingly strong NAVSIM performance and approaches leading camera-based methods like DrivoR [ref], suggesting that the benchmark does not strongly demand reactions to the current situation.
abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving models plan future trajectories from raw sensor input. While earlier driving benchmarks often measured deviation from the human trajectory, current benchmarks such as NAVSIM and Bench2Drive evaluate models with richer simulation-based metrics intended to capture safe and compliant driving. A high benchmark score should reflect that a model can understand the scene in front of it and act accordingly. But how much of that score specifically comes from reacting to the dynamic part of that scene? To probe this, we remove a model's camera input and replace it with memories from prior drives at the same location. The retrieved memories can provide persistent scene information, including road layout and location-conditioned regularities, but not the current traffic state. Surprisingly, memory is nearly sufficient on NAVSIM, reaching or even exceeding the performance of leading end-to-end methods without actually observing the evaluated scene. Our results suggest that a high NAVSIM score does not require a planner to react to the current traffic scene and should be treated with caution. This effect is benchmark-dependent: driving from memory causes substantially larger performance drops on Bench2Drive and RealEngine. We provide our code at https://github.com/boschresearch/MemoryDrivoR .
